claim: Single-molecule imaging provides a powerful way to study biochemical processes in live cells.
source: Single-molecule imaging provides a powerful way to study biochemical processes in live cells, yet it remains challenging to track single molecules while simultaneously detecting their interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of single-molecule imaging, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains challenging to track single molecules while simultaneously detecting their interactions.
source: Single-molecule imaging provides a powerful way to study biochemical processes in live cells, yet it remains challenging to track single molecules while simultaneously detecting their interactions.
evidence: This statement reflects a known limitation in the field, based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Rhodamine dyes exhibit proximity-assisted photoactivation (PAPA), in which one fluorophore (the 'sender') can reactivate a second fluorophore (the 'receiver') from a dark state.
source: Here, we describe a novel property of rhodamine dyes, proximity-assisted photoactivation (PAPA), in which one fluorophore (the 'sender') can reactivate a second fluorophore (the 'receiver') from a dark state.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented throughout the paper.

claim: PAPA requires proximity between the two fluorophores.
source: PAPA requires proximity between the two fluorophores, yet it operates at a longer average intermolecular distance than Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from linker constructs and self-cleaving peptide experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: PAPA operates at a longer average intermolecular distance than Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
source: PAPA requires proximity between the two fluorophores, yet it operates at a longer average intermolecular distance than Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing PAPA and FRET efficiency across different linker lengths in Figure 2.

claim: PAPA can be used in live cells to detect protein–protein interactions.
source: We show that PAPA can be used in live cells both to detect protein–protein interactions and to highlight a subpopulation of labeled protein complexes in which two different labels are in proximity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with the FRB-FKBP rapamycin-inducible interaction system in Figure 3.

claim: PAPA can be used to highlight a subpopulation of labeled protein complexes in which two different labels are in proximity.
source: We show that PAPA can be used in live cells both to detect protein–protein interactions and to highlight a subpopulation of labeled protein complexes in which two different labels are in proximity.
evidence: This is demonstrated with defined two-component mixtures in Figure 4.

claim: PAPA detected the expected correlation between androgen receptor self-association and chromatin binding at the single-cell level.
source: In proof-of-concept experiments, PAPA detected the expected correlation between androgen receptor self-association and chromatin binding at the single-cell level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Single-particle tracking (SPT) is a valuable approach for monitoring the motions of individual protein molecules.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) is a valuable approach for monitoring the motions of individual protein molecules (Chen et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2018; Heckert et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2021), but it does not distinguish compositionally and functionally distinct complexes of the same protein.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPT does not distinguish compositionally and functionally distinct complexes of the same protein.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) is a valuable approach for monitoring the motions of individual protein molecules (Chen et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2018; Heckert et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2021), but it does not distinguish compositionally and functionally distinct complexes of the same protein.
evidence: This is a known limitation of SPT, based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Two-color SPT can infer interactions between proteins when both partners are so dilute that they can be fully labeled while still resolving single molecules.
source: Two-color SPT can infer interactions between proteins when both partners are so dilute that they can be fully labeled while still resolving single molecules (Asher et al., 2021; Sotolongo Bellón et al., 2022; Wilmes et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: For most proteins, detection of single molecules requires sparse labeling, which makes double-labeled complexes exceedingly rare.
source: For most proteins, however, detection of single molecules requires sparse labeling, which makes double-labeled complexes exceedingly rare.
evidence: This is based on logical inference from the requirements of single-molecule imaging and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Single-molecule FRET is not in general a practical way to detect protein–protein interactions in live cells due to a requirement for sparse double-labeling, challenges with spectral crosstalk, and the large size of genetically encoded tags relative to the working distance of FRET.
source: Single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET), though powerful for monitoring intra-molecular conformational changes, is not in general a practical way to detect protein–protein interactions in live cells due to a similar requirement for sparse double-labeling, challenges with spectral crosstalk, and the large size of genetically encoded tags relative to the working distance of FRET (see Appendix 1; Quast and Margeat, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation and further elaborated in Appendix 1.

claim: Fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) can detect bulk molecular interactions.
source: Fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) can detect bulk molecular interactions, yet it does not provide spatial trajectories for individual molecules, which are useful for measuring such properties as chromatin residence time and anomalous diffusion (Hansen et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2017; Izeddin et al., 2014; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: FCCS does not provide spatial trajectories for individual molecules.
source: Fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) can detect bulk molecular interactions, yet it does not provide spatial trajectories for individual molecules, which are useful for measuring such properties as chromatin residence time and anomalous diffusion (Hansen et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2017; Izeddin et al., 2014; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a known limitation of FCCS based on established knowledge.

claim: Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) detects molecular interactions based on the reconstitution of a fluorescent protein or HaloTag from two split halves fused to interacting partners.
source: Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) detects molecular interactions based on the reconstitution of a fluorescent protein or HaloTag from two split halves fused to interacting partners (Ghosh et al., 2000; Hu et al., 2002; Kerppola, 2008; Makhija et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The extremely strong association of split proteins in BiFC perturbs the binding equilibrium of their interacting partners.
source: While BiFC can be combined with single-molecule imaging (Mao et al., 2021; Nickerson et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2021), a drawback of this approach is that the extremely strong association of split proteins perturbs the binding equilibrium of their interacting partners (Kerppola, 2008; Kodama and Hu, 2012; Nickerson et al., 2014), making it impossible to accurately measure dynamic interactions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The perturbation of binding equilibrium by BiFC makes it impossible to accurately measure dynamic interactions.
source: While BiFC can be combined with single-molecule imaging (Mao et al., 2021; Nickerson et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2021), a drawback of this approach is that the extremely strong association of split proteins perturbs the binding equilibrium of their interacting partners (Kerppola, 2008; Kodama and Hu, 2012; Nickerson et al., 2014), making it impossible to accurately measure dynamic interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about BiFC limitations.

claim: Exciting one cyanine dye can reactivate a nearby cyanine dye from a dark state.
source: An alternative in vitro proximity sensor to smFRET was devised by Bates, Blosser, and Zhuang, who observed that exciting one cyanine dye can reactivate a nearby cyanine dye from a dark state (Bates et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Photoswitching of cyanine dye pairs enabled early implementations of STORM imaging.
source: Although photoswitching of cyanine dye pairs enabled early implementations of STORM imaging (Rust et al., 2006), its application as a proximity sensor has been limited by the short inter-fluorophore distance required (≤2 nm), the poor cell permeability of cyanine dyes, and the need for high thiol concentrations and an oxygen-scavenging system (Chen et al., 2016; Geertsema et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The application of cyanine dye photoswitching as a proximity sensor has been limited by the short inter-fluorophore distance required (≤2 nm), the poor cell permeability of cyanine dyes, and the need for high thiol concentrations and an oxygen-scavenging system.
source: Although photoswitching of cyanine dye pairs enabled early implementations of STORM imaging (Rust et al., 2006), its application as a proximity sensor has been limited by the short inter-fluorophore distance required (≤2 nm), the poor cell permeability of cyanine dyes, and the need for high thiol concentrations and an oxygen-scavenging system (Chen et al., 2016; Geertsema et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many fluorophores—notably rhodamine dyes—can enter a dark state and be directly reactivated by short-wavelength (e.g., 405 nm) light.
source: However, many fluorophores—notably rhodamine dyes—can enter a dark state and be directly reactivated by short-wavelength (e.g., 405 nm) light (van de Linde et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Direct reactivation of rhodamine dyes has been employed for direct STORM (dSTORM) imaging in both live and fixed cells.
source: This phenomenon, which has been employed for direct STORM (dSTORM) imaging in both live and fixed cells (Grimm et al., 2015; Heilemann et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2021), is thought to involve conversion of excited triplet-state fluorophores to reduced species whose absorbance is shifted to shorter wavelengths (Bates et al., 2005; Dempsey et al., 2009; Gidi et al., 2020; Heilemann et al., 2008; van de Linde et al., 2011; Vaughan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Direct reactivation of rhodamine dyes is thought to involve conversion of excited triplet-state fluorophores to reduced species whose absorbance is shifted to shorter wavelengths.
source: This phenomenon, which has been employed for direct STORM (dSTORM) imaging in both live and fixed cells (Grimm et al., 2015; Heilemann et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2021), is thought to involve conversion of excited triplet-state fluorophores to reduced species whose absorbance is shifted to shorter wavelengths (Bates et al., 2005; Dempsey et al., 2009; Gidi et al., 2020; Heilemann et al., 2008; van de Linde et al., 2011; Vaughan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: The development of bright, cell-permeable Janelia Fluor (JF) dyes has transformed single-molecule imaging in live cells.
source: The development of bright, cell-permeable Janelia Fluor (JF) dyes, based on rhodamine and silicon-rhodamine chemical scaffolds, has transformed single-molecule imaging in live cells (Grimm et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Janelia Fluor X 650 (JFX650) can be reactivated from a dark state by excitation of a nearby fluorophore such as Janelia Fluor 549 (JF549).
source: Here, we show that Janelia Fluor X 650 (JFX650; Grimm et al., 2021) and similar fluorophores can be reactivated from a dark state by excitation of a nearby fluorophore such as Janelia Fluor 549 (JF549), a phenomenon which we term proximity-assisted photoactivation (PAPA).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: PAPA of JF dyes occurs under physiological conditions in live cells and requires neither an oxygen-scavenging system nor exogenous thiols.
source: In contrast to cyanine dye reactivation, PAPA of JF dyes occurs under physiological conditions in live cells and requires neither an oxygen-scavenging system nor exogenous thiols.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental conditions described in the Methods section and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: PAPA's effective distance range extends beyond that of FRET.
source: While PAPA requires proximity between the two fluorophores, its effective distance range extends beyond that of FRET, making it a potentially more versatile interaction sensor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing PAPA and FRET in Figure 2.

claim: PAPA can be used to detect the formation of protein dimers.
source: We show that PAPA can be used to detect the formation of protein dimers and that it can enrich for double-labeled molecules within defined mixtures, albeit not with perfect selectivity (see 'Discussion' and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with the FRB-FKBP system in Figure 3.

claim: PAPA can enrich for double-labeled molecules within defined mixtures, albeit not with perfect selectivity.
source: We show that PAPA can be used to detect the formation of protein dimers and that it can enrich for double-labeled molecules within defined mixtures, albeit not with perfect selectivity (see 'Discussion' and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4 with defined two-component mixtures.

claim: PAPA combined with SPT can analyze the increase in chromatin binding induced by self-association of androgen receptor.
source: As a further proof of concept, we combined SPT with PAPA to analyze the increase in chromatin binding induced by self-association of androgen receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5.

claim: Some JFX650 molecules that had gone dark during red illumination suddenly reappeared after a brief, 7 ms pulse of green light.
source: When we alternately excited JFX650 with red light (639 nm) and JF549 with green light (561 nm), we noticed that some JFX650 molecules that had gone dark during red illumination suddenly reappeared after a brief, 7 ms pulse of green light (green vertical lines in Figure 1ai and green box in Figure 1b, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1ai and 1b.

claim: Reactivation of JFX650 by violet light occurs both with and without JF549-HTL.
source: Consistent with previous work (Grimm et al., 2015), we also observed reactivation of JFX650 by violet light, both with and without JF549-HTL (violet vertical lines in Figure 1ai,ii and violet box in Figure 1b).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1ai, 1aii, and 1b, and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: Reactivation of JFX650 by green light required co-labeling with JF549.
source: However, reactivation of JFX650 by green light required co-labeling with JF549 (compare Figure 1ai and ii), implying that reactivation results not from direct absorption of green light by dark-state JFX650 but indirectly due to excitation of JF549.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1ai and 1aii.

claim: Reactivation of JFX650 by green light results not from direct absorption of green light by dark-state JFX650 but indirectly due to excitation of JF549.
source: However, reactivation of JFX650 by green light required co-labeling with JF549 (compare Figure 1ai and ii), implying that reactivation results not from direct absorption of green light by dark-state JFX650 but indirectly due to excitation of JF549.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that green reactivation requires JF549.

claim: Green illumination of cells labeled with JF549-HTL alone did not produce localizations in the JFX650 channel.
source: Green illumination of cells labeled with JF549-HTL alone did not produce localizations in the JFX650 channel, demonstrating that this effect is not due to JF549 photochromism (Figure 1aiii).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1aiii.

claim: The green reactivation effect is not due to JF549 photochromism.
source: Green illumination of cells labeled with JF549-HTL alone did not produce localizations in the JFX650 channel, demonstrating that this effect is not due to JF549 photochromism (Figure 1aiii).
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiment in Figure 1aiii.

claim: Violet reactivation was similar for both Halo-SNAPf and Halo-PT2A-SNAPf constructs.
source: While violet reactivation was similar for both constructs, green reactivation was substantially greater for Halo-SNAPf than for Halo-PT2A-SNAPf, implying that proximity of the two dyes facilitates reactivation by green light (Figure 1c).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Green reactivation was substantially greater for Halo-SNAPf than for Halo-PT2A-SNAPf.
source: While violet reactivation was similar for both constructs, green reactivation was substantially greater for Halo-SNAPf than for Halo-PT2A-SNAPf, implying that proximity of the two dyes facilitates reactivation by green light (Figure 1c).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Proximity of the two dyes facilitates reactivation by green light.
source: While violet reactivation was similar for both constructs, green reactivation was substantially greater for Halo-SNAPf than for Halo-PT2A-SNAPf, implying that proximity of the two dyes facilitates reactivation by green light (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of linked vs. cleaved constructs in Figure 1c.

claim: Conjugating JFX650 to SNAPf instead of Halo led to more efficient shelving in the dark state.
source: Conjugating JFX650 to SNAPf instead of Halo led to more efficient shelving in the dark state, as evidenced by a faster decline in fluorescence during red illumination and greater subsequent reactivation by violet light (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: JF549 is more photostable when bound to Halo than when bound to SNAP.
source: This accords with the previous observation that JF549 is more photostable when bound to Halo than when bound to SNAP (Presman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: About 10% of JFX650-SNAPf molecules enter the dark state under the experimental conditions and can be reactivated by either DR or PAPA.
source: Ensemble and single-molecule kinetic measurements indicate that about 10% of JFX650-SNAPf molecules enter the dark state under our experimental conditions and can be reactivated by either DR or PAPA (Figure 1—figure supplements 1b and 3).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1b and 3.

claim: DR by violet light precluded subsequent PAPA by green light, and vice versa.
source: DR by violet light precluded subsequent PAPA by green light, and vice versa, implying that both wavelengths reactivate the same dark state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Both violet and green wavelengths reactivate the same dark state.
source: DR by violet light precluded subsequent PAPA by green light, and vice versa, implying that both wavelengths reactivate the same dark state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutual occlusion experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: PAPA occurred when tetramethylrhodamine (TMR), Janelia Fluor X 549 (JFX549), or Janelia Fluor 526 were used as the sender.
source: We tested other fluorophore pairs and found that PAPA occurred when tetramethylrhodamine (TMR), Janelia Fluor X 549 (JFX549), or Janelia Fluor 526 were used as the sender, or when JF646 or JFX646 were used as the receiver (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PAPA occurred when JF646 or JFX646 were used as the receiver.
source: We tested other fluorophore pairs and found that PAPA occurred when tetramethylrhodamine (TMR), Janelia Fluor X 549 (JFX549), or Janelia Fluor 526 were used as the sender, or when JF646 or JFX646 were used as the receiver (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PAPA/DR ratio provides a normalized measure of PAPA efficiency.
source: The ratio of the increase in fluorescence intensity in response to green and violet pulses (the 'PAPA/DR ratio') provides a normalized measure of PAPA efficiency, which corrects for cell-to-cell variability in the labeled protein concentration.
evidence: This is a methodological definition based on the experimental design.

claim: For sufficiently short reactivation pulses, the PAPA/DR ratio increased linearly with the green pulse duration.
source: For sufficiently short reactivation pulses, the PAPA/DR ratio increased linearly with the green pulse duration (with the violet pulse duration held constant), making it possible to measure relative rate constants by linear fitting (Figure 2a, b, left panel).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b (left panel).

claim: FRET efficiency between JF549 and JFX650 declined sharply with increasing spacer length.
source: As predicted by our simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), FRET efficiency between JF549 and JFX650 declined sharply with increasing spacer length, from 0.271 ± 0.010 (95% CI) for the short linker to 0.124 ± 0.006 for a single Ig repeat and 0.020 ± 0.010 for three Ig repeats (Figure 2b, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by FLIM-FRET measurements shown in Figure 2b (right panel).

claim: FRET was essentially undetectable for five or seven Ig repeats and for the PT2A self-cleaving peptide linker.
source: FRET was essentially undetectable for five or seven Ig repeats and for the PT2A self-cleaving peptide linker (Figure 2b, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by FLIM-FRET measurements shown in Figure 2b (right panel).

claim: PAPA was observed for the 3×, 5×, and 7× Ig linker constructs.
source: In contrast, PAPA was observed for the 3×, 5×, and 7× Ig linker constructs (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: The rate of photoactivation by green light declined gradually with increasing linker length yet was distinguishable from the background rate of the PT2A self-cleaving linker.
source: The rate of photoactivation by green light declined gradually with increasing linker length yet was distinguishable from the background rate of the PT2A self-cleaving linker.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: PAPA has a less stringent dependence on average inter-fluorophore distance than FRET.
source: These results indicate that PAPA has a less stringent dependence on average inter-fluorophore distance than FRET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of PAPA and FRET data across different linker lengths in Figure 2.

claim: Addition of rapamycin caused a dramatic increase in the ratio of PAPA to DR.
source: Addition of rapamycin caused a dramatic increase in the ratio of PAPA (green reactivation) to DR (violet reactivation), consistent with ligand-induced dimerization of Halo-FRB and SNAPf-FKBP bringing together JF549 and JFX650 (Figure 3b and c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b, 3c, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The increase in PAPA/DR ratio upon rapamycin addition is consistent with ligand-induced dimerization of Halo-FRB and SNAPf-FKBP bringing together JF549 and JFX650.
source: Addition of rapamycin caused a dramatic increase in the ratio of PAPA (green reactivation) to DR (violet reactivation), consistent with ligand-induced dimerization of Halo-FRB and SNAPf-FKBP bringing together JF549 and JFX650 (Figure 3b and c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of rapamycin-induced FRB-FKBP dimerization and the observed increase in PAPA signal.

claim: PAPA trajectories were enriched for freely diffusing molecules compared to DR trajectories in the Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS + H2B-SNAPf mixture.
source: PAPA trajectories were enriched for freely diffusing molecules compared to DR trajectories, as expected if PAPA selectively reactivates JF549/JFX650 double-labeled Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS molecules (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by diffusion spectra shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PAPA trajectories had a lower bound fraction than DR trajectories in every cell for the Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS + H2B-SNAPf mixture.
source: Consistent with the ensemble analysis, PAPA trajectories had a lower bound fraction than DR trajectories in every cell (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: For the SNAPf-3xNLS + Halo-SNAPf-H2B mixture, PAPA trajectories were enriched in bound molecules compared to DR trajectories.
source: As expected, the opposite trend was observed: PAPA trajectories were enriched in bound molecules compared to DR trajectories, both across an ensemble of cells and at the single-cell level (Figure 4e and f, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4e, 4f, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d.

claim: PAPA and DR trajectories displayed virtually identical diffusion spectra for double-labeled Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS or Halo-SNAPf-H2B alone.
source: As a further control, we analyzed cells expressing JF549-HTL/JFX650-STL double-labeled Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS or Halo-SNAPf-H2B alone. As expected, PAPA and DR trajectories displayed virtually identical diffusion spectra for these individual components (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–f).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–f.

claim: For the cytosolic Halo-SNAPf + SNAPf-60-mer mixture, PAPA trajectories were strongly enriched in the fast-diffusing subpopulation compared to DR trajectories.
source: Compared to DR trajectories (violet curve), PAPA trajectories (green curve) were strongly enriched in the fast-diffusing subpopulation, consistent with selective reactivation of the double-labeled Halo-SNAPf protein by green light (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is supported by diffusion spectra shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The enrichment of the fast-diffusing population by PAPA was not absolute as a slow-diffusing shoulder peak was still observed among PAPA trajectories.
source: The enrichment of the fast-diffusing population was not absolute as a slow-diffusing shoulder peak was still observed among PAPA trajectories (Figure 4h, green curve; see 'Discussion').
evidence: This observation is evident in the diffusion spectrum shown in Figure 4h.

claim: For Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS + SNAPf-H2B, PAPA enriched double-labeled molecules approximately ninefold.
source: For Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS + SNAPf-H2B, the best fit was obtained for DR trajectories with a mixture of 53% Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS and 47% SNAPf-H2B, while the best fit for PAPA trajectories was obtained with 91% Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS and 9% SNAPf-H2B (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a). The estimated ratio of Halo-SNAPf-3xNLS to SNAPf-H2B thus increases from 0.53/0.47 ≈ 1.1 among DR trajectories to 0.91/0.09 ≈ 10 among PAPA trajectories, an approximately ninefold enrichment of double-labeled molecules by PAPA.
evidence: This is based on quantitative modeling of the diffusion spectra shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a.

claim: PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf-H2B over SNAPf-3xNLS by 3.7-fold.
source: Similar calculations showed that PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf-H2B over SNAPf-3xNLS by 3.7-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b), Halo-SNAPf over SNAPf-60mer by 7.6-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c), and Halo-SNAPf-60mer over SNAPf by 37-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is based on quantitative modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4b.

claim: PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf over SNAPf-60mer by 7.6-fold.
source: Similar calculations showed that PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf-H2B over SNAPf-3xNLS by 3.7-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b), Halo-SNAPf over SNAPf-60mer by 7.6-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c), and Halo-SNAPf-60mer over SNAPf by 37-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is based on quantitative modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4c.

claim: PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf-60mer over SNAPf by 37-fold.
source: Similar calculations showed that PAPA enriched Halo-SNAPf-H2B over SNAPf-3xNLS by 3.7-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b), Halo-SNAPf over SNAPf-60mer by 7.6-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c), and Halo-SNAPf-60mer over SNAPf by 37-fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is based on quantitative modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4d.

claim: PAPA enrichment was substantial—between 3.7- and 37-fold for different defined mixtures—but was not absolute.
source: While this enrichment was substantial—between 3.7- and 37-fold for different defined mixtures—it was not absolute, and thus it is crucial not to misinterpret PAPA trajectories as a pure sample of interacting molecules (see 'Discussion' and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the quantitative modeling results from Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Treatment with dihydrotestosterone (DHT) led to an increase in the ratio of PAPA to DR for androgen receptor over the course of several minutes.
source: As expected, treatment with the androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) led to an increase in the ratio of PAPA to DR over the course of several minutes (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), consistent with the two fluorophores being brought together by ligand-induced interaction between SNAPf-mAR and Halo-mAR.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The increase in PAPA/DR ratio for androgen receptor upon DHT treatment is consistent with the two fluorophores being brought together by ligand-induced interaction between SNAPf-mAR and Halo-mAR.
source: As expected, treatment with the androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) led to an increase in the ratio of PAPA to DR over the course of several minutes (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), consistent with the two fluorophores being brought together by ligand-induced interaction between SNAPf-mAR and Halo-mAR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in PAPA signal and known biology of androgen receptor.

claim: Addition of DHT caused an increase in the overall bound fraction of AR.
source: Consistent with previous biochemical and live-cell imaging experiments, addition of DHT caused an increase in the overall bound fraction of AR (Figure 5c and d; Schaufele et al., 2005; van Royen et al., 2007; van Royen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and 5d, and is consistent with cited previous literature.

claim: PAPA trajectories had a higher bound fraction than DR trajectories for androgen receptor, both before and after addition of DHT.
source: Strikingly, PAPA trajectories had a higher bound fraction than DR trajectories, both before and after addition of DHT (Figure 5c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: The higher bound fraction of PAPA trajectories for androgen receptor is consistent with an increase in the affinity of AR for specific DNA sequence motifs upon self-association.
source: This is consistent with an increase in the affinity of AR for specific DNA sequence motifs upon self-association.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between PAPA signal (indicating self-association) and chromatin binding.

claim: A subset of AR molecules self-associated and bound chromatin with elevated affinity even prior to addition of exogenous androgen.
source: Moreover, PAPA revealed that a subset of AR molecules self-associated and bound chromatin with elevated affinity even prior to addition of exogenous androgen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated PAPA signal and bound fraction before DHT addition in Figure 5c.

claim: The physical mechanism underlying PAPA remains unclear.
source: While the physical mechanism underlying PAPA remains unclear, its more flexible distance dependence than either FRET (Figure 2) or cyanine dye photoswitching (Bates et al., 2005) suggests a distinct process.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: One speculative hypothesis for PAPA mechanism is that the excited sender reacts with some other molecule in the cell, producing a short-lived chemical species that diffuses a limited distance to react with and reactivate the receiver dark state.

claim: PAPA circumvents the trade-off between labeling density and spectral crosstalk inherent in smFRET.

evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal separation of sender and receiver excitation in PAPA.

claim: In PAPA, sender and receiver excitation occur at different times, eliminating fluorescence bleed-through from the sender into the receiver channel.
source: In PAPA, sender and receiver excitation occur at different times, eliminating fluorescence bleed-through from the sender into the receiver channel.
